word_meanings.short_definition: To ask someone to come to an event or do something with you.
word_meanings.learner_definition: You can name the event after to, or use to plus a verb for the activity. The other person can accept or refuse.

word_meanings.short_definition: To take part in an activity with other people.
word_meanings.learner_definition: Use join plus a person or group when you want to do an activity with them. You can add for to name a meal or activity.

word_meanings.short_definition: Not busy and able to do something at a particular time.
word_meanings.learner_definition: Use available to ask whether a person has time for an activity. Say when, using a phrase such as on Saturday or after six.

word_meanings.short_definition: To give an idea for someone to consider.
word_meanings.learner_definition: A suggestion is an option for the group to discuss. After suggest, you can name an activity or use a verb ending in -ing.

word_meanings.short_definition: To plan and organize something that will happen.
word_meanings.learner_definition: Arranging a meeting can include choosing a time, finding a place and contacting the people who will come.

word_meanings.short_definition: To state that a planned time or arrangement is correct or definite.
word_meanings.learner_definition: You can check a detail such as the time or place, or say definitely that you will attend. Asking someone to confirm a plan helps everyone know what to expect.

word_meanings.short_definition: To change the time or date of a planned event.
word_meanings.learner_definition: The event is still planned, but it will happen at a different time. You can use for before the new day or time.

word_meanings.short_definition: To stop a planned event or arrangement from going ahead.
word_meanings.learner_definition: Cancelling a plan does not by itself give it a new time. You may make another plan later, but the original event is no longer going ahead.

word_meanings.short_definition: At the planned or expected time; not late.
word_meanings.learner_definition: Use on time when there is an expected arrival or start time. For a meeting at six, arriving on time means being there when the meeting is due to begin.

word_meanings.short_definition: Used to say that you like an idea or plan.
word_meanings.learner_definition: This friendly response can show agreement with a suggestion. You may still need to agree on details such as the time and place.

word_meanings.short_definition: To meet another person, usually to spend time together.
word_meanings.learner_definition: You can meet up with friends at a place or after an activity. Unlike catch up, meet up does not necessarily mean sharing news after time apart.

word_meanings.short_definition: To continue communicating with someone over time.
word_meanings.learner_definition: You can keep in touch by calling, messaging or meeting. The phrase is often used when people say goodbye and want to stay connected.

usage_notes.note_text: discuss salary expectations
Neutral; common in recruitment.
Use the plural expectations in this standard interview phrase.
casual conversation
Informal in tone but neutral as a description.
Casual describes a noun; casually is the adverb.
key stakeholder
Neutral; common business vocabulary.
A stakeholder can be affected by a project without owning company shares.
order take-out
Informal; takeaway is common in British English.
As a noun use take-out; the verb phrase is take out.
brainstorm ideas
Neutral to informal workplace language.
Brainstorm can take a direct object; brainstorm about is often unnecessary.
order an appetizer
Common in American English; starter is common in British English.
An appetizer comes before the main course, not after it.
go through a security check
Neutral; standard travel vocabulary.
Say go through security, not pass from security.
call the front desk
Neutral; reception is a common synonym.
Front desk names the service area, not the desk in a guest room.
make small talk
Neutral to informal.
Small talk is uncountable; do not say a small talk for one conversation.
read the menu
Neutral; standard restaurant vocabulary.
Menu refers to the list, not usually the individual meal ordered.
catch up with someone
Informal and friendly.
Use catch up as the verb; catch-up is the noun or adjective.
a follow-up meeting
Neutral; common business vocabulary.
Use follow-up for the noun or adjective and follow up for the verb.
send a follow-up
Neutral; common business vocabulary.
Use follow-up for the noun and follow up for the verb.
make a reservation
Neutral; booking is also common.
Use a reservation for the booking and reserve for the verb.
course syllabus
Neutral; standard academic vocabulary.
The common plurals are syllabuses and syllabi.
work on a group project
Neutral; standard academic vocabulary.
A group project is collaborative; an individual project is completed alone.
ask for the bill
Neutral; check is common in American restaurants.
Do not use receipt when asking how much you owe; the receipt comes after payment.
departure gate
Neutral; standard travel vocabulary.
At an airport, a gate is a boarding area, not only a physical door.
assign action items
Neutral; common workplace vocabulary.
Action items are specific tasks, not all topics discussed.
write a cover letter
Neutral; standard employment vocabulary.
A cover letter supports a resume; it does not replace it.
late check-out
Neutral; standard hotel vocabulary.
Use check-out for the noun and check out for the verb.
show a boarding pass
Neutral; standard travel vocabulary.
Do not confuse a boarding pass with a ticket, which confirms the booking.
set the agenda
Neutral; standard workplace vocabulary.
Agenda is singular in modern English; agendas is the plural.
a short layover
Neutral; stopover is also common.
A layover is between connecting flights, not the final destination.
provide references
Neutral; standard employment vocabulary.
A reference may mean the person or their recommendation; make the context clear.
exchange greetings
Neutral; the exact greeting may be formal or informal.
Greeting is the noun; greet is the verb.
complete an assignment
Neutral; standard academic vocabulary.
Assignment is countable; homework is usually uncountable.
meet a deadline
Neutral; standard workplace vocabulary.
You meet a deadline when on time and miss it when late.
leave a tip
Neutral; tipping customs vary by place.
A tip is extra money, while the bill is the amount charged.
check in luggage
Neutral; baggage is a common synonym.
Luggage is uncountable; say two pieces of luggage, not two luggages.
meet the qualifications
Neutral; standard employment vocabulary.
Qualifications are evidence of suitability, not only academic degrees.
say farewell
Farewell can sound formal or mark an important goodbye; Goodbye and See you are more usual between friends.
Use to before the person: say farewell to someone.
make weekend plans
Neutral and conversational.
Plans is usually plural when asking generally about someone's weekend; a weekend plan can refer to one specific plan.
hold office hours
Neutral; standard academic vocabulary.
Office hours is normally plural even when referring to a recurring period.
go through customs
Neutral; standard border-control vocabulary.
Customs takes a singular verb when it names the government service.
activate a key card
Neutral; standard hotel vocabulary.
Write key card as two words when it is a noun.
request a wake-up call
Neutral; standard hotel vocabulary.
Use wake-up with a hyphen before call; wake up is the verb phrase.
hotel amenities
Neutral; common in travel descriptions.
Amenities are useful features, not basic room furniture in general.
update a resume
Neutral; CV is used in many regions.
Resume without accents can also mean continue, so context matters.
confirm a reservation
Neutral; standard hotel vocabulary.
Use reservation for the booking and reserve for the action.
submission deadline
Neutral; standard academic vocabulary.
Use by before a deadline time, not until when stating the required submission time.
attend a lecture
Neutral; standard academic vocabulary.
A lecture is the teaching session, while a lecturer is the person.
invite someone to dinner; invite someone to do something
Would you like to...? is a friendly way to make the invitation itself.
Keep the person after invite: invite her to dinner, not invite to her dinner.
join us for lunch; join my friends for a walk
Can I join you? is a friendly way to ask to take part.
Join us for lunch is the usual invitation; no with is needed here.
available on Saturday; available after six; available for lunch
Free is a more informal alternative when talking about time.
Use a form of be: Are you available?, not Do you available?
suggest a picnic; suggest meeting at seven
Suggest is neutral; How about ...? is another common way to offer an idea in conversation.
Say suggest meeting, not suggest to meet, when the activity comes directly after suggest.
arrange a time; arrange a meeting; arrange to meet
Arrange is useful in everyday planning as well as at work.
Arrange to meet describes making the plan; it does not say that the meeting has already happened.
confirm the time; confirm that you can come
Confirm is useful when checking plans; Are we still meeting at seven? is a more casual question.
To confirm attendance is to say you will come; it does not mean you have already arrived.
reschedule lunch for Friday; reschedule a meeting
Could we reschedule...? is a polite way to ask for a change.
Reschedule changes when an event happens; cancel says it will not happen as planned.
cancel a picnic; cancel a booking
When changing plans with friends, a short explanation and an apology can help.
Cancelled and cancelling are usual British forms; canceled and canceling are usual American forms. Both spellings are valid.
arrive on time; start on time
On time is neutral and useful for both social and work plans.
On time means not late for the plan; in time for the film means early enough to see it.
That sounds good; sounds good to me
Sounds good! is a natural short response in friendly conversation and messages. In sentence practice, use a complete example such as That sounds good.
Use sounds good for a singular idea: That sounds good. With plural plans, use sound: Those plans sound good.
meet up with a friend; meet up outside the station
Meet up is informal and common when making social plans.
Use meet up with Ana, not meet Ana up. The past form is met up.
keep in touch with someone; keep in touch by email
Keep in touch! is a friendly goodbye, but it does not arrange a particular meeting.
Use with before the person: keep in touch with me. The past form is kept in touch.
Ask for a smaller or larger size. A size label does not guarantee that clothes will fit.
Use try on plus the clothes: try on a jacket. With a pronoun, say try it on.
Use fit plus a person: the shoes fit me. A colour or style that looks good on you suits you.
Keep a receipt as proof of payment. It is different from the bill you receive before paying.
Ask for a refund or receive a refund. A shop may have conditions for returning goods.
Use exchange something for something else. A refund gives money back instead of another item.
Here rent is a noun: pay the rent. To rent a flat uses the same spelling as a verb.
This word names the person or company renting out a property; it does not describe your rights or the rental agreement.
Here repair is a noun: a repair or repairs. You can also use repair as a verb: repair the door.
Use at the bus stop for the place where you wait. A large transport building may be a bus station.
In this travel meaning, schedule is another common word. Check which day the listed times apply to.
At a railway station, look for a platform number. This meaning is not an online service or a stage.
One-way ticket is another common term. A single ticket does not include the journey back.
Round-trip ticket is another common term. Check when and where the ticket can be used.
Use change trains or change buses without the. You can name the place with at: change at Central Station.
Package is another common word for something wrapped for delivery.
A postal address can include a building number, street, town and postal code. Share only the details needed for the delivery.
Use delivery of something or delivery to a place. Delivery dates describe when the goods are brought.
Cash is uncountable: some cash, not a cash. Notes are also called bills in American English.
This can include a debit or credit card. Never share a card number or security code in a practice sentence.
Common phrases include make a payment and receive a payment. Paid is the past form of the verb pay.
Fill in a form and fill out a form both mean providing the requested information.
Use sign as the verb: sign the form. Signature is the written name, not the action.
Line is another common word in this meaning. You can join a queue or wait in a queue.
Use make an appointment, have an appointment, or change an appointment. This word is also used for other arranged services.
Use describe your symptoms to talk about what you notice. Knowing this vocabulary does not identify an illness.
A pharmacist is the person trained to supply medicines and give advice; a pharmacy is the place or service.
Use a weak signal or no signal for a poor phone connection. This is different from the sound used for a notification.
Leave a voicemail means record a message for someone. Check your voicemail means listen to messages left for you.
Use call back after a time, or call someone back. With a pronoun, say call her back, not call back her.
Use an attachment for a file included with a message. It is not the main text of the email.
In a message, a link opens another online resource. Check that a message is trustworthy before opening its links.
Use reply to a message or reply to someone. The preposition to comes before the person or message.
Common phrases include the morning shift and the night shift. A shift is a work period, not a change of opinion here.
Use take a break or have a break. A lunch break is a pause in work for a meal.
Co-worker is another common word. This relationship does not necessarily mean the person is your manager or friend.
Here update is a noun: give an update on a project. To update a file uses the same spelling as a verb.
Use give a presentation on or about a topic. A talk can be a presentation even without slides.
